claim: Immune cells infiltrating tumors can have important impact on tumor progression and response to therapy.
source: Immune cells infiltrating tumors can have important impact on tumor progression and response to therapy.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that reflects established scientific understanding in the field of immuno-oncology.

claim: EPIC is an efficient algorithm to simultaneously estimate the fraction of cancer and immune cell types from bulk tumor gene expression data.
source: We present an efficient algorithm to simultaneously estimate the fraction of cancer and immune cell types from bulk tumor gene expression data.
evidence: This is the main claim of the paper describing the method developed by the authors.

claim: EPIC integrates novel gene expression profiles from each major non-malignant cell type found in tumors.
source: Our method integrates novel gene expression profiles from each major non-malignant cell type found in tumors, renormalization based on cell-type-specific mRNA content, and the ability to consider uncharacterized and possibly highly variable cell types.
evidence: The abstract describes the components of the EPIC method, which are detailed in the Results section with reference profiles shown in Supplementary files.

claim: EPIC includes renormalization based on cell-type-specific mRNA content.
source: Our method integrates novel gene expression profiles from each major non-malignant cell type found in tumors, renormalization based on cell-type-specific mRNA content, and the ability to consider uncharacterized and possibly highly variable cell types.
evidence: The abstract describes this feature, which is experimentally validated with mRNA measurements shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: EPIC has the ability to consider uncharacterized and possibly highly variable cell types.
source: Our method integrates novel gene expression profiles from each major non-malignant cell type found in tumors, renormalization based on cell-type-specific mRNA content, and the ability to consider uncharacterized and possibly highly variable cell types.
evidence: This is a key algorithmic feature described in the abstract and detailed in the Materials and methods section.

claim: EPIC was validated with flow cytometry of human melanoma tumor specimens.
source: Feasibility is demonstrated by validation with flow cytometry, immunohistochemistry and single-cell RNA-Seq analyses of human melanoma and colorectal tumor specimens.
evidence: The abstract states this validation approach, which is shown in Figure 3A with experimental data from four melanoma patients.

claim: EPIC was validated with immunohistochemistry of colorectal tumor specimens.
source: Feasibility is demonstrated by validation with flow cytometry, immunohistochemistry and single-cell RNA-Seq analyses of human melanoma and colorectal tumor specimens.
evidence: The abstract states this validation approach, which is shown in Figure 3B using publicly available IHC data from Becht et al., 2016.

claim: EPIC was validated with single-cell RNA-Seq analyses of human melanoma tumor specimens.
source: Feasibility is demonstrated by validation with flow cytometry, immunohistochemistry and single-cell RNA-Seq analyses of human melanoma and colorectal tumor specimens.
evidence: The abstract states this validation approach, which is shown in Figure 3C using data from Tirosh et al., 2016.

claim: Tumors form complex microenvironments composed of various cell types such as cancer, immune, stromal and endothelial cells.
source: Tumors form complex microenvironments composed of various cell types such as cancer, immune, stromal and endothelial cells (Hanahan and Weinberg, 2011; Joyce and Fearon, 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to established literature in cancer biology.

claim: Immune cells infiltrating the tumor microenvironment play a major role in shaping tumor progression, response to (immuno-)therapy and patient survival.
source: Immune cells infiltrating the tumor microenvironment play a major role in shaping tumor progression, response to (immuno-)therapy and patient survival (Fridman et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Fridman et al., 2012.

claim: Gene expression analysis is widely used to characterize tumors at the molecular level.
source: Today, gene expression analysis is widely used to characterize tumors at the molecular level.
evidence: This is a statement about current practice in cancer research, reflecting established knowledge in the field.

claim: Tumor gene expression profiles from tens of thousands of patients are available across all major tumor types in databases such as Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) or The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA).
source: As a consequence, tumor gene expression profiles from tens of thousands of patients are available across all major tumor types in databases such as Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO [Edgar et al., 2002]) or The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA [Hoadley et al., 2014]).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to the GEO and TCGA databases.

claim: Flow cytometry or immunohistochemistry measurements to quantify the number of both malignant and tumor-infiltrating immune cells are rarely performed for samples analyzed at the gene expression level.
source: Unfortunately, flow cytometry or immunohistochemistry (IHC) measurements to quantify the number of both malignant and tumor-infiltrating immune cells are rarely performed for samples analyzed at the gene expression level.
evidence: This is an observation about current research practices that motivates the need for computational methods.

claim: Some bioinformatics methods aim at estimating tumor purity based on copy number variation but do not provide information about the different immune cell types.
source: Some aim at estimating tumor purity based on copy number variation (Carter et al., 2012; Li and Li, 2014), or expression data (Ahn et al., 2013; Clarke et al., 2010; Quon et al., 2013; Yoshihara et al., 2013), but do not provide information about the different immune cell types.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to multiple methods and describes their limitations.

claim: Some bioinformatics methods focus on predicting the relative proportions of cell types by fitting reference gene expression profiles from sorted cells.
source: Others focus on predicting the relative proportions of cell types by fitting reference gene expression profiles from sorted cells (Gong and Szustakowski, 2013; Li et al., 2016; Newman et al., 2015; Qiao et al., 2012) or with the help of gene signatures (Becht et al., 2016; Zhong et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to multiple existing methods.

claim: None of the existing methods provides quantitative information about both cancer and non-malignant cell type proportions directly from tumor gene expression profiles.
source: However, none of these methods provides quantitative information about both cancer and non-malignant cell type proportions directly from tumor gene expression profiles.
evidence: This is a critical assessment of existing methods that identifies a gap in the field.

claim: Reference gene expression profiles used in previous studies have been mainly obtained from circulating immune cells sorted from peripheral blood.
source: In addition, reference gene expression profiles used in previous studies have been mainly obtained from circulating immune cells sorted from peripheral blood and were generally based on microarrays technology.
evidence: This is an observation about the limitations of previous approaches.

claim: Reference gene expression profiles used in previous studies were generally based on microarrays technology.
source: In addition, reference gene expression profiles used in previous studies have been mainly obtained from circulating immune cells sorted from peripheral blood and were generally based on microarrays technology.
evidence: This is an observation about the technology used in previous approaches.

claim: Several cell fraction prediction approaches have not been experimentally validated in solid tumors from human patients.
source: Finally, several of these approaches have not been experimentally validated in solid tumors from human patients.
evidence: This is a critical assessment of existing methods identifying a limitation.

claim: EPIC is based on a unique collection of RNA-Seq reference gene expression profiles from either circulating immune cells or tumor-infiltrating non-malignant cell types.
source: EPIC is based on a unique collection of RNA-Seq reference gene expression profiles from either circulating immune cells or tumor- infiltrating non-malignant cell types (i.e., immune, stromal and endothelial cells).
evidence: This describes the data used to build the EPIC method, which is detailed in the Results section and Supplementary files.

claim: EPIC accounts for the high variability of cancer cells across patients and tissue of origin by implementing the ability to consider uncharacterized, possibly highly variable, cell types.
source: To account for the high variability of cancer cells across patients and tissue of origin, we implemented in our algorithm the ability to consider uncharacterized, possibly highly variable, cell types.
evidence: This describes a key algorithmic feature of EPIC that addresses a specific challenge.

claim: EPIC predictions were validated in human solid tumors by analyzing melanoma samples with both flow cytometry and RNA-Seq.
source: To validate our predictions in human solid tumors, we first analyzed melanoma samples with both flow cytometry and RNA-Seq.
evidence: This describes the validation approach, with results shown in Figure 3A.

claim: EPIC predictions were validated using publicly available IHC data of colorectal tumors.
source: We then collected publicly available IHC and single-cell RNA-Seq data of colorectal and melanoma tumors.
evidence: This describes the validation approach, with results shown in Figure 3B using data from Becht et al., 2016.

claim: EPIC predictions were validated using publicly available single-cell RNA-Seq data of melanoma tumors.
source: We then collected publicly available IHC and single-cell RNA-Seq data of colorectal and melanoma tumors.
evidence: This describes the validation approach, with results shown in Figure 3C using data from Tirosh et al., 2016.

claim: All three validation datasets showed that very accurate predictions of both cancer and non-malignant cell type proportions could be obtained even in the absence of a priori information about cancer cells.
source: All three validation datasets showed that very accurate predictions of both cancer and non-malignant cell type proportions could be obtained even in the absence of a priori information about cancer cells.
evidence: This is a summary of the validation results shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: EPIC incorporates reference gene expression profiles from each major immune and other non-malignant cell type to model bulk RNA-Seq data as a superposition of these reference profiles.
source: EPIC incorporates reference gene expression profiles from each major immune and other non-malignant cell type to model bulk RNA-Seq data as a superposition of these reference profiles (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: This describes the mathematical approach of EPIC, illustrated in Figure 1A,B.

claim: RNA-Seq profiles of various human innate and adaptive circulating immune cell types were collected and curated from CD4 T cells, CD8 T cells, B cells, NK cells, Monocytes and Neutrophils.
source: To tailor our predictions to recent gene expression studies, we first collected and curated RNA-Seq profiles of various human innate and adaptive circulating immune cell types (Hoek et al., 2015; Linsley et al., 2014; Pabst et al., 2016) (CD4 T cells, CD8 T cells, B cells, NK cells, Monocytes and Neutrophils) from a diverse set of patients analyzed in different centers (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This describes the data collection for building reference profiles, with citations to the source studies.

claim: Principal component analysis of circulating immune cell RNA-Seq data showed that samples clustered first according to cell type and not according to experiment of origin, patient age, disease status or other factors.
source: Principal component analysis (PCA) of these data (Figure 1C) showed that samples clustered first according to cell type and not according to experiment of origin, patient age, disease status or other factors, suggesting that they could be used as bona fide reference expression profiles across different patients.
evidence: This is an observation from the PCA analysis shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Circulating immune cell samples could be used as bona fide reference expression profiles across different patients.
source: Principal component analysis (PCA) of these data (Figure 1C) showed that samples clustered first according to cell type and not according to experiment of origin, patient age, disease status or other factors, suggesting that they could be used as bona fide reference expression profiles across different patients.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the PCA analysis shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Reference gene expression profiles for each major immune cell type were built from RNA-Seq samples based on the median normalized counts per gene and cell type.
source: Reference gene expression profiles for each major immune cell type were built from these RNA-Seq samples based on the median normalized counts per gene and cell type.
evidence: This describes the method for constructing reference profiles, with values provided in Supplementary file 1.

claim: The variability in expression for each gene was considered when predicting the various cell proportions based on reference profiles.
source: The variability in expression for each gene was also considered when predicting the various cell proportions based on these reference profiles (see Materials and methods and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This describes a feature of the EPIC algorithm detailed in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Immune cells differ in their gene expression profiles depending on their state and site of origin (e.g., blood or tumors).
source: Immune cells differ in their gene expression profiles depending on their state and site of origin (e.g., blood or tumors) (Ganesan et al., 2017; Speiser et al., 2016; Zheng et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to three studies.

claim: Reference gene expression profiles of tumor-infiltrating immune cell types (CD4 T, CD8 T, B, NK, macrophages) were established.
source: To study the potential effect of these differences on our predictions, we established reference gene expression profiles of each major tumor-infiltrating immune cell type (i.e., CD4 T, CD8 T, B, NK, macrophages).
evidence: This describes the establishment of tumor-infiltrating cell reference profiles from single-cell RNA-Seq data.

claim: Reference profiles for stromal cells (cancer-associated fibroblasts) and endothelial cells were derived.
source: We further derived reference profiles for stromal cells (i.e. cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs)) and endothelial cells.
evidence: This describes additional reference profiles established for non-immune cell types.

claim: Reference gene expression profiles of tumor-infiltrating cells were obtained as cell type averages from single-cell RNA-Seq data of melanoma patients from Tirosh and colleagues.
source: These reference gene expression profiles were obtained as cell type averages from the single-cell RNA-Seq data of melanoma patients from Tirosh and colleagues (Tirosh et al., 2016), considering only samples from primary tumor and non-lymphoid tissue metastasis (see Materials and methods and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This describes the source and method for constructing tumor-infiltrating cell reference profiles.

claim: Principal component analysis of tumor-infiltrating cells' gene expression profiles showed that samples clustered first according to cell type.
source: As for circulating immune cell data, principal component analysis of the tumor-infiltrating cells' gene expression profiles showed that samples clustered first according to cell type (Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1, see also results in [Tirosh et al., 2016]).
evidence: This is an observation from the PCA analysis shown in Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Reference gene expression profiles from each immune and other non-malignant cell types were used to model bulk gene expression data as a linear combination of m different cell types.
source: Reference gene expression profiles from each of the immune and other non-malignant (i.e., stromal and endothelial) cell types were then used to model bulk gene expression data as a linear combination of m different cell types (Figure 1B).
evidence: This describes the mathematical modeling approach of EPIC, illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: EPIC implements the ability to consider an uncharacterized cell population to include cell types like cancer cells that show high variability across patients and tissues of origin.
source: To include cell types like cancer cells that show high variability across patients and tissues of origin, we further implemented in our algorithm the ability to consider an uncharacterized cell population.
evidence: This describes a key algorithmic feature of EPIC.

claim: EPIC takes advantage of the presence of gene markers of non-malignant cells that are not expressed in cancer cells.
source: Mathematically this was done by taking advantage of the presence of gene markers of non-malignant cells that are not expressed in cancer cells.
evidence: This describes the mathematical approach used in EPIC to handle uncharacterized cell types.

claim: EPIC does not require signature genes to be expressed in exactly one cell type, but only to show very low expression in cancer cells.
source: Importantly, we do not require our signature genes to be expressed in exactly one cell type, but only to show very low expression in cancer cells.
evidence: This describes a feature of the signature gene selection in EPIC.

claim: The mRNA proportion of each immune and other non-malignant cell type was inferred using least-square regression.
source: The mRNA proportion of each immune and other non-malignant cell type was inferred using least-square regression, solving first our system of equations for the marker genes (green box in Figure 1B, see Materials and methods).
evidence: This describes the mathematical method used in EPIC.

claim: The fraction of cancer cells was determined as one minus the fraction of all non-malignant cell types.
source: The fraction of cancer cells was then determined as one minus the fraction of all non-malignant cell types.
evidence: This describes how cancer cell fraction is calculated in EPIC.

claim: Cell markers used in EPIC were determined by differential expression analysis based on reference cell gene expression profiles as well as gene expression data from non-hematopoietic tissues.
source: Cell markers used in this work were determined by differential expression analysis based on our reference cell gene expression profiles as well as gene expression data from non-hematopoietic tissues (see Materials and methods and Appendix 1—table 1).
evidence: This describes the method for selecting signature genes, with results in Appendix 1—table 1.

claim: EPIC measured the mRNA content of all major immune cell types as well as of cancer cells to enable meaningful comparison with flow cytometry and IHC data.
source: Finally, to account for different amounts of mRNA in different cell types and enable meaningful comparison with flow cytometry and IHC data, we measured the mRNA content of all major immune cell types as well as of cancer cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 2) and used these values to renormalize our predicted mRNA proportions (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This describes an experimental measurement performed to improve EPIC predictions, shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: EPIC was tested using three datasets comprising bulk RNA-Seq data from PBMC or whole blood with corresponding proportions of immune cell types determined by flow cytometry.
source: We first tested our algorithm using three datasets comprising bulk RNA-Seq data from PBMC (Hoek et al., 2015; Zimmermann et al., 2016) or whole blood (Linsley et al., 2014), as well as the corresponding proportions of immune cell types determined by flow cytometry (Figure 2A).
evidence: This describes the validation approach in blood samples, with results shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Very accurate predictions were obtained by EPIC when fitting reference profiles from circulating immune cells in blood samples.
source: Overall, very accurate predictions were obtained by fitting reference profiles from circulating immune cells, considering either all cell types together (Figure 2A) or each cell type separately (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a summary of the validation results shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: EPIC showed clear improvement compared to other widely used cell fraction prediction methods when tested on blood samples.
source: When comparing with other widely used cell fraction prediction methods (Becht et al., 2016; Gong and Szustakowski, 2013; Li et al., 2016; Newman et al., 2015; Quon et al., 2013; Zhong et al., 2013), we observed a clear improvement (Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a comparative analysis shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The renormalization by mRNA content appeared to be important for predicting actual cell fractions.
source: The renormalization by mRNA content, which had not been considered in previous approaches, appeared to be important for predicting actual cell fractions (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is an observation from the comparison shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Most other cell fraction prediction methods could benefit from mRNA renormalization step.
source: Moreover, we observed that most other methods could also benefit from such a renormalization step, be it for the global prediction of all cell types together or for the predictions of each cell type (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is an observation from the analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: A conceptually related approach to EPIC's renormalization was developed by Baron et al. (2016) for pancreatic cells.
source: A conceptually related approach was developed by Baron et al. (2016), but the rescaling was done on the gene expression reference profiles (in their case of pancreatic cells) based on the total number of transcripts per cell type and the prediction of the proportion of pancreatic cells from a bulk sample was carried out with CIBERSORT (Newman et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a comparison with a related method, supported by citations.

claim: EPIC with a priori renormalization step showed similar results to a posteriori renormalization.
source: For comparison purpose, we implemented such an a priori renormalization step in EPIC as well, and observed similar results than with the a posteriori renormalization (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a comparison of different renormalization approaches shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: EPIC allows for a cell type without a known reference gene expression profile.
source: With respect to the other methods, EPIC has two other main distinctive features: (i) it allows for a cell type without a known reference gene expression profile (such a feature is also part of ISOpure [Quon et al., 2013]) and (ii) it integrates information about the variability in each signature gene from the reference gene expression profiles.
evidence: This describes a key feature of EPIC, with comparison to ISOpure.

claim: EPIC integrates information about the variability in each signature gene from the reference gene expression profiles.
source: With respect to the other methods, EPIC has two other main distinctive features: (i) it allows for a cell type without a known reference gene expression profile (such a feature is also part of ISOpure [Quon et al., 2013]) and (ii) it integrates information about the variability in each signature gene from the reference gene expression profiles.
evidence: This describes a key feature of EPIC.

claim: Integrating gene expression variability slightly improves the prediction accuracy but to a lesser extent than the renormalization by mRNA.
source: The latter point slightly improves the prediction accuracy but to a lesser extent than the renormalization by mRNA (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is an observation from the analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: When T cell subsets were removed from reference gene expression profiles, EPIC results remained nearly unchanged while other methods suffered from this.
source: As expected, the results from EPIC including or not the T cell reference profiles remained nearly unchanged, while the other methods suffered from this, except for DSA (Zhong et al., 2013) which is based only on signature genes and not reference profiles (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is an observation from the analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: Single cell suspensions were collected from lymph nodes of four metastatic melanoma patients for validation.
source: To validate our predictions in tumors, we collected single cell suspensions from lymph nodes of four metastatic melanoma patients (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This describes the experimental validation approach in tumor samples.

claim: A fraction of the melanoma cell suspension was used to measure different cell type proportions with flow cytometry and the other fraction was used for bulk RNA sequencing.
source: A fraction of the cell suspension was used to measure the different cell type proportions with flow cytometry (CD4 T, CD8 T, B, NK, melanoma and other cells comprising mostly stromal and endothelial cells; Supplementary file 3A), and the other fraction was used for bulk RNA sequencing (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes the experimental design for validation, illustrated in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: A remarkable agreement was observed between EPIC predictions and experimentally determined cell fractions in melanoma lymph node samples.
source: We observed a remarkable agreement between our predictions and experimentally determined cell fractions (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a summary of the validation results shown in Figure 3A.

claim: All predicted cell proportions from EPIC fall nearly on the 'y = x' line in melanoma lymph node samples.
source: This clearly indicates that the absolute cell fractions were correctly predicted for all cell types, as confirmed by a low RMSE.
evidence: This is an observation from Figure 3A about the accuracy of predictions.

claim: The proportion of melanoma cells could be very accurately predicted even in the absence of a priori information about their gene expression.
source: Of note, the proportion of melanoma cells could be very accurately predicted even in the absence of a priori information about their gene expression.
evidence: This is an important observation from the validation in Figure 3A demonstrating a key capability of EPIC.

claim: EPIC predictions showed significant correlation with immunohistochemistry data from colon cancer primary tumors.
source: Although a limited number of immune cell types had been assayed in this study, we observed a significant correlation between cell proportions measured by IHC and our predictions, except for the CD8 T cells (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a summary of the validation results shown in Figure 3B using data from Becht et al., 2016.

claim: EPIC predictions were consistent with observed cell fractions from single-cell RNA-Seq data of melanoma samples.
source: Here again, our predictions were consistent with the observed cell fractions, even for melanoma cells for which we did not assume any reference gene expression profile (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a summary of the validation results shown in Figure 3C using data from Tirosh et al., 2016.

claim: The predicted cell fractions from melanoma cells and all other immune cell types fall nearly on the y = x line in single-cell RNA-Seq validation.
source: Notably, the predicted cell fractions from melanoma cells as well as from all other immune cell types fall nearly on the y = x line, showing that not only the relative cell type proportions could be predicted but also the absolute proportions for all cell types.
evidence: This is an observation from Figure 3C about the accuracy of predictions.

claim: For single-cell RNA-Seq validation, a leave-one-out procedure was applied to avoid using the same samples both to build the reference profiles and the bulk RNA-Seq data.
source: For the single-cell RNA-Seq data (Figure 4C), we applied a leave-one-out procedure, to avoid using the same samples both to build the reference profiles and the bulk RNA-Seq data used as input for the predictions (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This describes the validation methodology to avoid circularity.

claim: Predictions did not change much when using tumor-infiltrating cell reference profiles compared to circulating immune cell reference profiles.
source: Overall, predictions did not change much compared to those based on circulating immune cell reference gene expression profiles (Figure 4), except for the IHC data where the predictions for CD8 T cells and macrophages clearly improved (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a comparison of results using different reference profiles, shown in Figure 4.

claim: Predictions for CD8 T cells and macrophages clearly improved with tumor-infiltrating cell reference profiles for IHC data.
source: Overall, predictions did not change much compared to those based on circulating immune cell reference gene expression profiles (Figure 4), except for the IHC data where the predictions for CD8 T cells and macrophages clearly improved (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is an observation from the comparison shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Predictions for CD8 T cells and macrophages improved in datasets of primary tumors and non-lymph node metastases but not in datasets from lymph node metastases when using tumor-infiltrating cell reference profiles.
source: Moreover, we could observe some differences between the results obtained from circulating immune cell reference gene expression profiles and those from tumor-infiltrating cell reference gene expression profiles, when considering the proportions from each cell type independently (Figures 3–4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1): (i) predictions for CD8 T cells and macrophages improved in the datasets of primary tumors and non-lymph node metastases but not in the datasets from lymph node metastases
evidence: This is an observation from the comparison shown in Figures 3-4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Predictions for B and NK cells displayed similar accuracy based on circulating cells or tumor-infiltrating cells profiles for all datasets.
source: (ii) predictions for B and NK cells displayed similar accuracy based on the circulating cells or tumor-infiltrating cells profiles for all datasets
evidence: This is an observation from the comparison shown in Figures 3-4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The proportion of CAFs and endothelial cells could be well predicted based on reference profiles constructed from tumor-infiltrating cells.
source: and (iii) CAFs and endothelial cells were not available for the blood-based reference profiles but the proportion of these cells could be well predicted based on the reference profiles constructed from tumor-infiltrating cells (Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an observation from the results shown in Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: EPIC displayed improved accuracy compared to ISOpure in all three validation datasets.
source: EPIC displayed improved accuracy in all three datasets (Figure 5A, and Figure 5—figure supplements 1–4).
evidence: This is a comparison with ISOpure shown in Figure 5A and supplementary figures.

claim: Predictions from EPIC were in general more accurate than other methods, especially when considering all cell types together.
source: Predictions from EPIC were in general more accurate, especially when considering all cell types together.
evidence: This is a summary of the benchmarking results shown in Figure 5.

claim: When restricting comparisons to relative cell type proportions, some methods like MCPcounter and TIMER showed similar accuracy as EPIC for the cell types considered in these methods.
source: Nevertheless, when restricting the comparisons to relative cell type proportions, some methods like MCPcounter (Becht et al., 2016) and TIMER (Li et al., 2016) were quite consistent in their predictions across the various datasets and showed similar accuracy as EPIC for the cell types considered in these methods (Figure 5—figure supplements 1–4).
evidence: This is an observation from the benchmarking analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplements 1–4.

claim: MCPcounter could not be included in the global prediction comparison as this method returns scores that are not comparable between different cell types.
source: Of note, MCPcounter could not be included in the global prediction comparison as this method returns scores that are not comparable between different cell types.
evidence: This is an observation about the limitations of MCPcounter for certain comparisons.

claim: Predictions from DSA were quite accurate when available, but in multiple cases some cell type proportions returned by the method were simply equal to 0 in all samples.
source: Predictions from DSA (Zhong et al., 2013) were also quite accurate when available, but in multiple cases some cell type proportions returned by the method were simply equal to 0 in all samples (Figure 5—figure supplements 1–4 – correlation values were replaced by NA in these cases).
evidence: This is an observation about the limitations of DSA shown in Figure 5—figure supplements 1–4.

claim: ESTIMATE immune, stromal and tumor purity scores were correlated with the total fraction of immune cells, stromal cells and the fraction of cancer cells, but correlation was not significant for the tumor purity score.
source: Immune, stromal and tumor purity scores (Yoshihara et al., 2013) based on gene set enrichment analysis were also correlated with the total fraction of immune cells, stromal cells and the fraction of cancer cells (correlation was not significant for the tumor purity score – Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is a comparison with ESTIMATE shown in Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 5.

claim: Correlations from ESTIMATE were considerably lower than those obtained with EPIC.
source: However, these correlations were considerably lower than those obtained with our approach (Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is a comparison with ESTIMATE shown in Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 5.

claim: ESTIMATE scores are less quantitative and more difficult to interpret with respect to actual cell type proportions.
source: Moreover, such scores are less quantitative and are thus more difficult to interpret with respect to actual cell type proportions.
evidence: This is an assessment of the limitations of ESTIMATE compared to EPIC.

claim: CD4+ Treg and Thelper cells were identified based on single-cell RNA-seq data from Tirosh and colleagues.
source: Based on the single-cell RNA-seq data from Tirosh and colleagues (Tirosh et al., 2016), we identified CD4+ Treg and Thelper cells (see Materials and methods), and built reference gene expression profiles for these cell types as we had done for the other cell types.
evidence: This describes an exploratory analysis to test prediction of T cell subsets.

claim: Significant correlations were observed for Treg and Thelper predictions, but the R-values are lower than for major cell types.
source: We observed significant correlations, but the R-values are lower than before (Figure 5—figure supplement 6), suggesting that we may be reaching the limits of cell fraction prediction methods for cell types that show lower abundance and substantial transcriptional similarity.
evidence: This is an observation from the analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 6.

claim: CIBERSORT using either the LM22 signature or newly derived signature did not perform better than EPIC for Treg and Thelper predictions.
source: Of note, CIBERSORT using either the LM22 signature or our newly derived signature did not perform better than EPIC.
evidence: This is a comparison with CIBERSORT for T cell subset predictions.

claim: EPIC overcomes several limitations of previous approaches by combining RNA-Seq profiles of all major immune and other non-malignant cell types from both circulating and tumor-infiltrating cells together with information about cell morphology (mRNA content) and algorithmic developments to consider uncharacterized cell types.
source: By combining RNA-Seq profiles of all major immune and other non-malignant cell types established from both circulating and tumor-infiltrating cells together with information about cell morphology (i.e., mRNA content) and algorithmic developments to consider uncharacterized and possibly highly variable cell types, EPIC overcomes several limitations of previous approaches to predict the fraction of both cancer and immune or other non-malignant cell types from bulk tumor gene expression data.
evidence: This is a summary statement about the advantages of EPIC over previous methods.

claim: EPIC takes advantage of the fact that cancer cells, in general, express no or only low levels of immune and stromal markers.
source: From an algorithmic point of view, EPIC takes advantage of the fact that cancer cells, in general, express no or only low levels of immune and stromal markers.
evidence: This describes a key assumption underlying the EPIC algorithm.

claim: EPIC can be broadly applied to most solid tumors, as confirmed by validation in melanoma and colorectal samples.
source: Therefore the method can be broadly applied to most solid tumors, as confirmed by our validation in melanoma and colorectal samples, but it will not be suitable for hematological malignancies like leukemia or lymphoma.
evidence: This is a statement about the applicability of EPIC based on the validation results.

claim: EPIC will not be suitable for hematological malignancies like leukemia or lymphoma.
source: Therefore the method can be broadly applied to most solid tumors, as confirmed by our validation in melanoma and colorectal samples, but it will not be suitable for hematological malignancies like leukemia or lymphoma.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of EPIC based on its algorithmic assumptions.

claim: The accuracy of predictions for some cell types might be sensitive to the origin or condition of the immune cells used for establishing reference profiles.
source: The accuracy of the predictions for some cell types might be sensitive to the origin or condition of the immune cells used for establishing reference profiles.
evidence: This is a discussion of factors affecting prediction accuracy.

claim: CD8 T cells and macrophages from primary tumors and non-lymph node metastases samples were best predicted using reference profiles from tumor-infiltrating cells.
source: For instance, we observed that CD8 T cells and macrophages from primary tumors and non-lymph node metastases samples were best predicted using the reference profiles from tumor-infiltrating cells.
evidence: This is an observation from the validation results comparing different reference profiles.

claim: The reference profiles from circulating cells corresponded to resting CD8 T cells and monocytes as only few activated CD8 T cells and no macrophages are circulating in blood.
source: This may be explained by the fact that the reference profiles from circulating cells corresponded to resting CD8 T cells and monocytes as only few activated C8 T cells and no macrophages are circulating in blood.
evidence: This is an explanation for the observed differences in prediction accuracy based on biological knowledge.

claim: For primary tumors or non-lymphoid tissue metastases, reference gene expression profiles from tumor-infiltrating immune cells are more appropriate.
source: Overall, our results suggest that for primary tumors or non-lymphoid tissue metastases reference gene expression profiles from tumor-infiltrating immune cells are more appropriate, while for lymph node metastases, profiles from either circulating or tumor-infiltrating immune cells could be used.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the validation results.

claim: For lymph node metastases, profiles from either circulating or tumor-infiltrating immune cells could be used.
source: Overall, our results suggest that for primary tumors or non-lymphoid tissue metastases reference gene expression profiles from tumor-infiltrating immune cells are more appropriate, while for lymph node metastases, profiles from either circulating or tumor-infiltrating immune cells could be used.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the validation results.

claim: One known limitation of cell fraction predictions arises when some cell types are present at very low frequency.
source: One known limitation of cell fraction predictions arises when some cell types are present at very low frequency (Shen-Orr and Gaujoux, 2013).
evidence: This is a discussion of a known limitation, supported by a citation.

claim: Predictions of cell proportions are reliable within an absolute error of about 8%, as estimated by the root mean squared error.
source: Our results suggest that predictions of cell proportions are reliable within an absolute error of about 8%, as estimated by the root mean squared error (Figure 3 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is an estimate of prediction accuracy based on the validation results shown in Figure 3 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The 8% error estimate is consistent with the lower detection limit proposed by other groups.
source: These estimates are consistent with the lower detection limit proposed by other groups (Becht et al., 2016; Zhong et al., 2013) and may explain why the relative proportions of NK cells, which are present at lower frequency in melanoma tumors (Balch et al., 1990; Sconocchia et al., 2012), could not be predicted with accuracy comparable to other cell types (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a comparison with other studies and an explanation for NK cell prediction accuracy, supported by citations.

claim: Another limitation of cell fraction predictions arises when considering cell types that show high transcriptional similarity.
source: Another limitation of cell fraction predictions arises when considering cell types that show high transcriptional similarity.
evidence: This is a discussion of another limitation of cell fraction prediction methods.

claim: Treg could not be well predicted by either EPIC or CIBERSORT because the gene expression profiles of Thelper and Treg are highly similar.
source: For instance, Treg in Figure 5—figure supplement 6 could not be well predicted neither by EPIC nor CIBERSORT. This can be understood because the gene expression profiles of Thelper and Treg are highly similar with only a few genes expressed differently between the two, making it harder for cell fraction prediction methods to work accurately.
evidence: This is an explanation for the poor prediction of Treg based on the analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 6.

claim: Treg were present at a proportion lower than 10% in all samples.
source: In addition, Treg were present at a proportion lower than 10% in all samples (Supplementary file 3E).
evidence: This is an observation from the data in Supplementary file 3E.

claim: For cell types with high transcriptional similarity and low abundance, gene set enrichment approaches may be more convenient than cell fraction prediction methods.
source: For such cases, gene set enrichment approaches, although less quantitative, may be more convenient, possibly combining them with the predictions obtained by EPIC for the main immune cell types.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the limitations observed for predicting similar cell types.

claim: EPIC predictions for the fraction of uncharacterized cells may include non-malignant cells, such as epithelial cells from neighboring tissues in addition to cancer cells.
source: Our predictions for the fraction of uncharacterized cells may include non-malignant cells, such as epithelial cells from neighboring tissues in addition to cancer cells.
evidence: This is a discussion of a potential limitation of EPIC.

claim: Compared to algorithms that first predict tumor purity based on exome sequencing data and later infer the relative fraction of immune cell types, EPIC predictions for immune and stromal cells are likely more quantitative.
source: Compared to recent algorithms that first predict tumor purity based on exome sequencing data, and later infer the relative fraction of immune cell types (Li et al., 2016), the predictions of EPIC for immune and stromal cells are likely more quantitative because they can implicitly consider the presence of not only cancer cells but also other non-malignant cells for which reference profiles are not available.
evidence: This is a comparison with other methods, supported by a citation.

claim: EPIC does not require both exome and RNA-Seq data from the same tumor samples, thereby reducing the cost and amount of experimental work for prospective studies.
source: Moreover, EPIC does not require both exome and RNA-Seq data from the same tumor samples, thereby reducing the cost and amount of experimental work for prospective studies, and broadening the scope of retrospective analyses of cancer genomics data to studies that only include gene expression data.
evidence: This is a statement about the practical advantages of EPIC.

claim: Recent technical developments in single-cell RNA-Seq technology enable researchers to directly access information about both the proportion of all cell types together with their gene expression characteristics.
source: Recent technical developments in single-cell RNA-Seq technology enable researchers to directly access information about both the proportion of all cell types together with their gene expression characteristics (Carmona et al., 2017; Efroni et al., 2015; Jaitin et al., 2014; Singer et al., 2016; Stegle et al., 2015; Tirosh et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a statement about single-cell RNA-Seq technology, supported by citations.

claim: Single-cell RNA-Seq data are much richer than anything that can be obtained with computational deconvolution of bulk gene expression profiles.
source: Such data are much richer than anything that can be obtained with computational deconvolution of bulk gene expression profiles and this technology may eventually replace standard gene expression analysis of bulk tumors.
evidence: This is a comparison between single-cell RNA-Seq and bulk RNA-Seq analysis.

claim: Single-cell RNA-Seq of human tumors is still logistically and technically very challenging due to high level of cell death upon sample manipulation and high transcript dropout rates.
source: Nevertheless, it is important to realize that, even when disregarding the financial aspects, single-cell RNA-Seq of human tumors is still logistically and technically very challenging due to high level of cell death upon sample manipulation (especially freezing and thawing) and high transcript dropout rates (Finak et al., 2015; Saliba et al., 2014; Stegle et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a discussion of the limitations of single-cell RNA-Seq, supported by citations.

claim: Some cells may better survive the processing with microfluidics devices used in some single-cell RNA-Seq platforms, thereby biasing the estimates of cell type proportions.
source: Moreover, one cannot exclude that some cells may better survive the processing with microfluidics devices used in some single-cell RNA-Seq platforms, thereby biasing the estimates of cell type proportions.
evidence: This is a discussion of a potential bias in single-cell RNA-Seq.

claim: Bulk tumor gene expression analysis will likely remain widely used for several years.
source: It is therefore likely that bulk tumor gene expression analysis will remain widely used for several years.
evidence: This is a prediction about the future use of bulk RNA-Seq based on current limitations of single-cell RNA-Seq.

claim: Recent single-cell RNA-Seq data of tumors obtained from a few patients can be exploited to refine cell fraction predictions in other patients that could not be analyzed with this technology.
source: Our work shows how we can exploit recent single-cell RNA-Seq data of tumors obtained from a few patients to refine cell fraction predictions in other patients that could not be analyzed with this technology, thereby overcoming some limitations of previous computational approaches that relied only on reference gene expression profiles from circulating immune cells.
evidence: This is a summary of how EPIC leverages single-cell RNA-Seq data to improve predictions.

claim: A detailed and biologically relevant validation of EPIC predictions was provided using actual tumor samples from human patients analyzed with flow cytometry, IHC and single-cell RNA-Seq.
source: In this work, we provide a detailed and biologically relevant validation of our predictions using actual tumor samples from human patients analyzed with flow cytometry, IHC and single-cell RNA-Seq.
evidence: This is a summary of the validation approach used in the study.

claim: The slightly lower agreement between EPIC predictions and IHC data may be partly explained by the fact that the exact same samples could not be used for both gene expression and IHC analyses.
source: We note that the slightly lower agreement between our predictions and IHC data may be partly explained by the fact that the exact same samples could not be used for both gene expression and IHC analyses because of the incompatibility between the two techniques.
evidence: This is a discussion of a limitation in the IHC validation.

claim: The overall high accuracy of EPIC predictions indicates that infiltrations of major immune cell types can be quantitatively studied directly from bulk tumor gene expression data.
source: Nevertheless, the overall high accuracy of our predictions indicates that infiltrations of major immune cell types can be quantitatively studied directly from bulk tumor gene expression data using computational approaches such as EPIC.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the validation results.

claim: EPIC can be downloaded as a standalone R package.
source: EPIC can be downloaded as a standalone R package (https://github.com/GfellerLab/EPIC/releases/tag/v1.1) (Racle, 2017) and can be used with reference gene expression profiles pre-compiled from circulating or tumor-infiltrating cells, or provided by the user.
evidence: This is information about the availability of EPIC.

claim: EPIC is available as a web application at http://epic.gfellerlab.org.
source: EPIC is also available as a web application (http://epic.gfellerlab.org) where users can upload bulk samples gene expression data and perform the full analysis.
evidence: This is information about the availability of EPIC.

claim: EPIC has been written as an R package and is freely available on GitHub for academic non-commercial research purposes.
source: EPIC has been written as an R package. It is freely available on GitHub (https://github.com/GfellerLab/EPIC; copy archived on https://github.com/elifesciences-publications/EPIC) for academic non-commercial research purposes.
evidence: This is information about the availability and licensing of EPIC.

claim: Version v1.1 of the EPIC package was used for the analyses in this study.
source: Version v1.1 of the package was used for our analyses.
evidence: This specifies the version of EPIC used in the study.

claim: In EPIC, the gene expression of a bulk sample is modeled as the sum of the gene expression profiles from the pure cell types composing this sample.
source: In EPIC, the gene expression of a bulk sample is modeled as the sum of the gene expression profiles from the pure cell types composing this sample (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: This describes the mathematical model underlying EPIC.

claim: EPIC works with RNA-seq data normalized into transcripts per million (TPM).
source: EPIC works with RNA-seq data, which is implicitly normalized. We use data normalized into transcripts per million (TPM) because it has some properties needed for the full cell proportion prediction to work, as will be shown in the next paragraphs.
evidence: This describes the data normalization used in EPIC.

claim: EPIC solves the system of equations for a subset of signature genes that are expressed by reference cell types but only expressed at a negligible level in uncharacterized cells.
source: Using these normalized quantities, EPIC then solves Equation (3) for a subset of ns equations corresponding to the ns signature genes (S) that are expressed by one or more of the reference cell types but only expressed at a negligible level in the uncharacterized cells (Figure 1B).
evidence: This describes the mathematical approach of EPIC.

claim: Previous computational work showed that the proportion from uncharacterized cells in bulk samples could be inferred with help of genes not expressed by the uncharacterized cells.
source: Previous computational work (Clarke et al., 2010; Gosink et al., 2007) showed that the proportion from uncharacterized cells in bulk samples could indeed be inferred with help of genes not expressed by the uncharacterized cells.
evidence: This is a citation to previous work supporting the approach used in EPIC.

claim: Cell-specific signature genes are well established and widely used in flow cytometry to sort immune cells.
source: Importantly, cell-specific signature genes are well established and widely used in flow cytometry to sort immune cells.
evidence: This is a statement about the biological basis for using signature genes.

claim: The solution to the EPIC equation can be estimated by a constrained least square optimization.
source: The solution to Equation (6) can be estimated by a constrained least square optimization.
evidence: This describes the mathematical method used in EPIC.

claim: EPIC takes advantage of the known variability for each gene in the reference profile to give weights in the function to minimize.
source: EPIC takes advantage of the known variability for each gene in the reference profile, to give weights in the function to minimize
evidence: This describes a feature of the EPIC algorithm.

claim: The weights in EPIC give more importance to signature genes with low variability in the reference gene expression profiles.
source: Here, the weights, wi, give more importance to the signature genes with low variability in the reference gene expression profiles.
evidence: This describes how weights are used in the EPIC algorithm.

claim: Patients agreed to donate metastatic tissues upon informed consent, based on dedicated clinical investigation protocols established according to the relevant regulatory standards.
source: Patients agreed to donate metastatic tissues upon informed consent, based on dedicated clinical investigation protocols established according to the relevant regulatory standards.
evidence: This describes the ethical approval for the study.

claim: The protocols were approved by the local IRB, the 'Commission cantonale d'éthique de la recherche sur l'être humain du Canton de Vaud'.
source: The protocols were approved by the local IRB, that is, the 'Commission cantonale d'éthique de la recherche sur l'être humain du Canton de Vaud'.
evidence: This describes the ethical approval for the study.

claim: Lymph nodes were obtained from stage III melanoma patients by lymph node dissection that took place before systemic treatment.
source: Lymph nodes (LN) were obtained from stage III melanoma patients, by lymph node dissection that took place before systemic treatment.
evidence: This describes the sample collection for the validation study.

claim: Single cell suspensions were obtained by mechanical disruption and immediately cryopreserved in RPMI 1640 supplemented with 40% FCS and 10% DMSO.
source: Single cell suspensions were obtained by mechanical disruption and immediately cryopreserved in RPMI 1640 supplemented with 40% FCS and 10% DMSO.
evidence: This describes the sample processing method.

claim: A dead cell removal kit (Miltenyi Biotech) was used to remove dead cells after thawing to limit their number.
source: In order to limit the number of dead cells after thawing, we removed those cells using a dead cell removal kit (Miltenyi Biotech).
evidence: This describes a step in the sample processing method.

claim: RNA-Seq data from the melanoma validation experiment have been deposited in NCBI's Gene Expression Omnibus and are accessible through GEO Series accession number GSE93722.
source: RNA-Seq data from this experiment have been deposited in NCBI's Gene Expression Omnibus (Edgar et al., 2002) and are accessible through GEO Series accession number GSE93722 (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/geo/query/acc.cgi?acc=GSE93722).
evidence: This describes the data availability for the study.

claim: Healthy donor peripheral blood was obtained through the blood transfusion center in Lausanne for mRNA content measurements.
source: Healthy donor peripheral blood was obtained through the blood transfusion center in Lausanne.
evidence: This describes the sample source for mRNA content measurements.

claim: PBMCs were purified by density gradient using Lymphoprep.
source: PBMCs were purified by density gradient using Lymphoprep (Axis-Shieldy).
evidence: This describes a step in the sample processing method.

claim: 1 × 10^6 live cells from each cell type were sorted using the BD FACS ARIA III for mRNA content measurements.
source: 1 × 106 live cells from each cell type were sorted using the BD FACS ARIA III (BD Biosciences).
evidence: This describes the cell sorting method for mRNA content measurements.

claim: The mRNA content for cancer cells was estimated from flow cytometry data using the forward scatter width, which is a good proxy of cell size and mRNA content.
source: The mRNA content for the cancer cells was estimated from the flow cytometry data described in the previous section from the four patients with melanoma. For this we used the forward scatter width, which is a good proxy of cell size and mRNA content (Padovan-Merhar et al., 2015; Tzur et al., 2011), and observed that cancer cells had similar amount of mRNA than B, NK and T cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This describes the method for estimating cancer cell mRNA content, supported by citations.

claim: A value of 0.4 pg of mRNA per cancer cell was used in EPIC.
source: We thus used a value of 0.4 pg of mRNA per cancer cell.
evidence: This describes a parameter value used in EPIC based on experimental measurements.

claim: RNA-seq reads alignment to the human genome (hg19) and TPM quantification were performed with RSEM version 1.2.19, using Bowtie2 version 2.2.4 and Samtools version 1.2.
source: RNA-seq reads alignment to the human genome, hg19, and TPM quantification were performed with RSEM (Li and Dewey, 2011) version 1.2.19, using Bowtie2 (Langmead and Salzberg, 2012) version 2.2.4 and Samtools (Li et al., 2009) version 1.2.
evidence: This describes the bioinformatics pipeline used for RNA-Seq data processing.

claim: Reference gene expression profiles of sorted immune cells from peripheral blood were built from datasets 2, 3 and 4.
source: Reference gene expression profiles of sorted immune cells from peripheral blood were built from the datasets 2, 3 and 4 described in previous section.
evidence: This describes the data sources for building reference profiles.

claim: No experimental biases were present in the circulating immune cell data as verified through unsupervised clustering with principal component analysis.
source: We verified no experimental biases were present in these data through unsupervised clustering of the samples, with help of a principal component analysis based on the normalized expression from the 1000 most variable genes (Figure 1C).
evidence: This describes a quality control analysis shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The median value of TPM counts was computed per cell type and per gene for the circulating immune cell reference profiles.
source: The median value of TPM counts was computed per cell type and per gene.
evidence: This describes the method for constructing reference profiles.

claim: The interquartile range of the TPM counts was computed per cell type and gene as a measure of the variability of each gene expression in each cell type.
source: Similarly, the interquartile range of the TPM counts was computed per cell type and gene, as a measure of the variability of each gene expression in each cell type.
evidence: This describes the method for quantifying gene expression variability in reference profiles.

claim: Granulocytes from dataset 4 and neutrophils from datasets 2 and 3 were combined to build the reference profile for neutrophils.
source: Granulocytes from dataset 4 and neutrophils from datasets 2 and 3 were combined to build the reference profile for neutrophils (neutrophils constitute more than 90% of granulocytes).
evidence: This describes how the neutrophil reference profile was constructed.

claim: No reference profile was built for myeloid dendritic cells as only few samples of these sorted cells existed and they were all from the same experiment.
source: No reference profile was built for the myeloid dendritic cells as only few samples of these sorted cells existed and they were all from the same experiment.
evidence: This explains why myeloid dendritic cells were not included in the reference profiles.

claim: The monocyte reference gene expression profile was used as a proxy for macrophages when applying EPIC to tumor samples.
source: Monocytes are not found in tumors but instead there are macrophages, mostly from monocytic lineage, that are infiltrating tumors and that are not found in blood. For this reason, we also used the monocyte reference gene expression profile as a proxy for macrophages when applying EPIC to tumor samples.
evidence: This describes an assumption made in EPIC based on biological knowledge.

claim: Using monocyte reference profile as a proxy for macrophages gave coherent results as observed in the validation.
source: Such an assumption gave coherent results as observed in the results.
evidence: This is an observation from the validation results supporting the use of monocyte profiles for macrophages.

claim: Tumor-infiltrating cell reference profiles were built based on the mean and standard deviation instead of median and interquartile range due to the nature of single-cell RNA-Seq data and gene dropout.
source: These reference profiles (Supplementary file 2) were built in the same way as described above for the reference profiles of circulating immune cells, but based on the mean and standard deviation instead of median and interquartile range respectively, due to the nature of single-cell RNA-Seq data and gene dropout present with such technique.
evidence: This describes a methodological adaptation for single-cell RNA-Seq data.
